questions.title: Why does the Federal Circuit apply Fifth Circuit law to JMOL and new-trial issues in a patent appeal?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the standard of review discussion at the beginning of the opinion. This is a patent case in the Federal Circuit, but the court says it reviews the denial of JMOL and the denial of a new trial under Fifth Circuit law, while it reviews claim construction under Federal Circuit law. How does that split work? Is the idea that some issues are considered 'procedural' and therefore governed by the regional circuit, while patent-specific substantive issues stay under Federal Circuit precedent? If so, where exactly is the line drawn?

questions.title: When can an appellate court treat expert testimony as too contradictory to support a jury verdict?
questions.question_body: The court says Finesse's expert gave 'confusing and unclear' testimony and relies on Johns Hopkins to hold that no reasonable jury could find infringement based on self-contradictory expert testimony. I'm struggling with that. Usually I thought credibility and weighing conflicting testimony are for the jury. So what makes this different? Is the rule that a jury can choose between two competing experts, but cannot rely on one expert whose own testimony defeats his infringement theory? How inconsistent does the testimony have to be before it stops being substantial evidence?

questions.title: Why wasn't it enough for the jury to infer that x1 and x2 were the claimed 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals'?
questions.question_body: On the '134 patent, the Federal Circuit seems to say the expert expressly mapped the claimed 'interference generating signals' to the 'modeled PIM path,' which was a problem because that path is generated only after sampling. But the district court thought he was 'clearly referring to x1 and x2' when talking about the two signals entering the RF ADC. Why couldn't the jury make that inference from the overall testimony and the diagram? Is the problem that the inference required too much reconstruction by counsel/court after the fact, rather than an actual claim-by-claim mapping presented to the jury?

questions.title: Why didn't changing the claim from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' create prosecution disclaimer?
questions.question_body: For the '775 patent, I expected the amendment history to be fatal. The original claims apparently said 'two or three signals,' the examiner rejected them over Filipovic, and the applicant amended the claims to require 'three signals S1, S2 and S3.' My instinct is that this should surrender systems using only two unique input signals. But the Federal Circuit says there was no 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal because the applicant also distinguished Filipovic on the ground that it addressed active rather than passive IMPs. How can an applicant make a narrowing amendment like that and still avoid disclaimer? Is the court distinguishing between amendment-based estoppel/disclaimer and mere evidence of what the claims require?

questions.title: What is the legal difference between 'three separately identifiable signals' and 'three unique signals'?
questions.question_body: The district court construed 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' to mean 'separately identifiable,' but not necessarily 'unique.' I'm not sure I understand what that means in practice. If a system has only two underlying input signals, how can it still have three separately identifiable signals? Does this mean one of the signals can just be a copy or repetition of another, as long as it plays a distinct role in the multiplication terms? And is that a normal way courts read signal-processing claim language, or was it specific to this patent's intrinsic and extrinsic evidence?

questions.title: Why were three distinct multiplication expressions not enough to satisfy a claim listing seven multiplications?
questions.question_body: The court ultimately reverses on the '775 patent because the accused radios only showed three distinct multiplications, while the claim required generating an n-th order ICS by multiplying and filtering seven listed products (S1×S1×S2, S1×S2×S2, etc.). The district court seemed to think three distinct products could still correspond to the seven claimed products if some terms overlap when signals are not unique. Why did the Federal Circuit reject that? If S1, S2, and S3 are not required to be unique, wouldn't some of the seven listed products collapse into the same expression? Or is the court saying that, even if some terms could theoretically overlap, the patentee still had to prove at trial exactly how the accused system performed all seven claimed multiplications?

questions.title: Why did the court vacate the damages award instead of deciding whether the damages trial was flawed?
questions.question_body: The appellants also challenged the damages award and asked for JMOL or at least a new trial on damages, but after reversing on infringement the Federal Circuit just vacates the $166 million award. Is that because once all asserted claims are found not infringed, the damages issues become moot? If so, is 'vacated' the normal disposition rather than 'reversed' for damages, and does that leave any damages rulings with precedential or preclusive effect if the case were somehow revived later?
